_comment: SOURCE CONTENT for the Unveil digital companion. This file is the single source of truth.
SLUGS ARE PERMANENT. A slug is baked into a printed QR code the moment the physical deck
goes to press. Changing one silently breaks that card forever. You may freely edit headline
and clue text; never edit a slug, and never reuse a retired one.
This file is NOT deployed. `npm run build` reads it and emits dist/, which contains only
encrypted card payloads. Keep this file out of the public web root.

cards.headline: A hospital itemised a new father's bill with a $39.35 charge for “skin to skin after C-section” — a fee for holding his own newborn.
clues: Precedent
Itemised hospital bills in private healthcare systems routinely contain micro-charges for standard nursing support that patients never review line by line.
Context
The father posted a photo of the receipt in 2016. The hospital confirmed the charge, explaining it covered the extra nurse required to monitor the infant in theatre.
Defense
It sounds like satire precisely because billing has reached the point of itemising a parent holding their child. The hospital's own defence of the charge is what makes it credible.

cards.headline: Scientists taught goldfish to drive a motorised robotic vehicle across a room toward targeted food rewards on land.
clues: Precedent
Behavioural neuroscientists routinely test spatial mapping across species using land-based apparatus to separate locomotion mechanics from pure navigation skill.
Context
Published in 2022 by researchers at an Israeli university, using a “fish-operated vehicle” — a tank on wheels that moved according to where the fish swam.
Defense
Frame it as legitimate ethology: the researchers isolated the fish's ability to navigate visually toward a target in an environment its species never evolved for.

cards.headline: A commercial airliner was delayed for hours because a swarm of roughly 20,000 bees settled on the plane's wing.
clues: Precedent
Aircraft are uniquely vulnerable to wildlife anomalies. Ground crews handle bird strikes constantly, but a swarm settling on an aerodynamic surface halts everything.
Context
It happened at a Houston airport gate in 2024. Staff could not simply spray them — a beekeeper was called to relocate the swarm intact.
Defense
A queen had likely landed on the warm wing and the colony followed her. No airline will taxi with 20,000 insects on a control surface.

cards.headline: Venice banned tourists from feeding pigeons in St Mark's Square, shutting down the birdseed vendors who had operated there for generations.
clues: Precedent
Historic European tourist sites absorb millions in structural damage and cleaning costs annually from invasive urban bird populations.
Context
The ban took effect in 2008. Officials cited the corrosive damage pigeon droppings inflict on marble and the cost of restoring the Basilica's stonework.
Defense
The city weighed the cleaning bill against the tourism value of the birds and found the pigeons were a net loss. Heritage economics, not whimsy.

cards.headline: The Australian military deployed soldiers with machine guns against a population of emus, and withdrew in defeat.
clues: Precedent
Interwar agricultural governments treated crop-destroying wildlife as a logistics problem and reached for military solutions when civilian control failed.
Context
In 1932, Western Australian wheat farmers petitioned for help against roughly 20,000 emus. Soldiers with Lewis guns were sent; the operation was called off.
Defense
Lean on the specific detail — the birds dispersed into small groups, defeating weapons designed for massed targets. Documented military history, not folklore.

cards.headline: A tavern in Japan employs macaque monkeys as waiters, who deliver drinks to customers and are paid in soybeans.
clues: Precedent
Japan has a long tradition of trained-monkey performance, and animal-welfare rules there set working-hour limits that the tavern openly observes.
Context
The Kayabukiya Tavern in Utsunomiya has done this for years. The monkeys wear uniforms, carry hot towels and drink orders, and work legally restricted short shifts.
Defense
Point at the regulatory detail. A fabricated story would not include working-hour limits — the mundane bureaucracy is the tell that it is real.

cards.headline: A storage tank burst in Boston and sent a wave of molasses through the streets at around 35 km/h, killing 21 people.
clues: Precedent
Early-20th-century industrial tanks were built without engineering review. Catastrophic failure of bulk liquid storage was a recognised hazard of the era.
Context
January 1919, in the North End. The tank held around 2.3 million gallons. The resulting lawsuit became a landmark case in industrial safety regulation.
Defense
Argue from the physics: molasses is far denser than water, so the wave carried enormous momentum. The absurdity of the substance says nothing about the deaths.

cards.headline: New Zealand passed a law granting a river the same legal rights as a human being, with appointed guardians who can sue on its behalf.
clues: Precedent
Legal systems already grant personhood to non-humans — corporations have held it for over a century.
Context
The Whanganui River received legal personhood in 2017, concluding one of the country's longest-running Māori legal claims. Two guardians represent it.
Defense
Reframe it as property law rather than mysticism: personhood gives the river standing in court, which no environmental statute had managed to provide.

cards.headline: In Switzerland it is illegal to keep a single guinea pig, because solitude is considered a form of animal abuse.
clues: Precedent
Several European states regulate the psychological welfare of pets, not merely their physical care.
Context
Swiss animal-welfare rules classify guinea pigs as social animals that must be kept in pairs. This created a small industry renting companions for bereaved survivors.
Defense
Lead with the rent-a-guinea-pig detail. It sounds like a joke, which is why players assume it is fabricated — but it is a direct market response to the regulation.

cards.headline: Denmark maintains an official government list of approved baby names, and parents wanting anything else must apply for permission.
clues: Precedent
Naming law is a real and unglamorous branch of civil administration across the Nordic countries and Iceland.
Context
The list runs to tens of thousands of pre-approved names. Applications outside it are reviewed for whether the name would subject the child to ridicule.
Defense
Frame it as child-protection law rather than authoritarianism. The stated purpose is preventing parents from burdening a child with a name they cannot escape.

cards.headline: An Alaskan town elected a cat as its honorary mayor, a position he held for twenty years.
clues: Precedent
Small unincorporated towns with no actual mayoral office frequently create ceremonial titles as tourism draws.
Context
Stubbs held the honorary post in Talkeetna, Alaska, from 1997 until his death in 2017. The town has no formal mayor, which is exactly why the title was available.
Defense
Emphasise the loophole — no governmental power was ever transferred to a cat. That distinction is what makes the story survive fact-checking.

cards.headline: A brown bear was formally enlisted in the Polish army during the Second World War, given a rank, and carried artillery ammunition in combat.
clues: Precedent
Military units have kept mascots for centuries. The unusual step here was formal enlistment, taken to solve a paperwork problem.
Context
Wojtek was enlisted so he could travel on a troopship that barred animals. He was given a name, rank and serial number, and served at Monte Cassino in 1944.
Defense
The bureaucratic motive is the proof. Nobody fabricating a story invents “we made him a private so he'd count as cargo” — that is how real institutions behave.

cards.headline: A penguin living in a Scottish zoo has been knighted and promoted to brigadier in the Norwegian King's Guard.
clues: Precedent
Ceremonial military patronage of animals is a live tradition in several European armies, complete with formal promotion parades.
Context
Sir Nils Olav is the regimental mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard, based at Edinburgh Zoo. He was knighted in 2008 with the approval of the King of Norway.
Defense
Point to the parade footage and the royal approval. This is a documented state ceremony, not a zoo publicity stunt.

cards.headline: A government poll to name a polar research vessel was won by “Boaty McBoatface”, and officials overruled the public result.
clues: Precedent
Open internet naming polls have been hijacked repeatedly. Agencies now write override clauses into the rules in advance.
Context
The 2016 UK poll drew over 120,000 votes for the joke name. The ship was named after a broadcaster instead, and the winning name went to one of its submarines.
Defense
The compromise is the credible part. A fabricated story would end at the humiliation — real institutions negotiate their way out.

cards.headline: The United States government stores over a billion pounds of surplus cheese in limestone caves in Missouri.
clues: Precedent
Agricultural price-support programmes have generated enormous state-held commodity surpluses for decades. The storage has to go somewhere.
Context
The caves are naturally cool former mines used as commercial cold storage. The stockpile grew out of dairy subsidies that bought excess production to hold prices stable.
Defense
Argue the economics: it is cheaper to warehouse surplus milk as cheese than to let dairy prices collapse. The cave is the least expensive refrigerator available.

cards.headline: The Netherlands closed prisons for lack of inmates and rented cells to Norway and Belgium to keep them staffed.
clues: Precedent
Prison capacity is a fixed cost. Closing a facility means losing trained staff who cannot be recalled when demand returns.
Context
Falling crime rates and sentencing policies favouring alternatives left Dutch facilities under-occupied. Several were leased to neighbouring states.
Defense
Frame it as workforce protection, not a stunt. The alternative was making prison officers redundant in regions with no other employer.

cards.headline: Sweden imports hundreds of thousands of tonnes of garbage from other countries because it does not produce enough of its own to fuel its power plants.
clues: Precedent
Waste-to-energy incineration is standard district-heating infrastructure across Scandinavia, and those plants require a continuous fuel supply.
Context
Aggressive domestic recycling reduced Sweden's burnable waste below plant capacity. Neighbouring countries pay Sweden to take waste they would otherwise landfill.
Defense
Sweden is paid twice — once to accept the waste, once for the heat it generates. The apparent absurdity is a functioning business model.

cards.headline: A university experiment started in 1927 has produced nine drops of liquid in a century, and nobody witnessed one fall until a webcam caught it.
clues: Precedent
Long-duration materials experiments exist specifically to measure properties too slow to observe within a human career.
Context
The pitch drop experiment at an Australian university shows that pitch, which shatters like a solid when struck, is a fluid of extraordinary viscosity.
Defense
The detail that sells it is the failure — decades of missed drops, including one lost to a coffee break. Fabrications do not include that kind of anticlimax.

cards.headline: A species of jellyfish can reverse its own ageing, reverting to its juvenile stage and starting its life cycle over, apparently without limit.
clues: Precedent
Cellular reprogramming is an established biological mechanism. Several species regenerate whole body structures from differentiated tissue.
Context
Turritopsis dohrnii transforms adult cells back to an earlier type and settles into a polyp colony under stress. It remains vulnerable to predation and disease.
Defense
Draw the distinction between immortal and invulnerable. The precision of the claim is evidence it came from a paper rather than a rumour.

cards.headline: Finland hosts an annual Wife Carrying World Championship where the winner receives their partner's weight in beer.
clues: Precedent
Regional Nordic sporting championships built around deliberately absurd disciplines are a well-established summer tourism format.
Context
The event runs in Sonkajärvi with formal international rules: a minimum carried weight, a standard obstacle course, and a time penalty for dropping your partner.
Defense
Lead with the rulebook. A joke does not need a minimum weight requirement and a drop penalty — a sanctioned competition does.

cards.headline: Global coffee shortage imminent as Brazil implements a 50% export ban to prioritise domestic reserves amid climate anomalies.
clues: Precedent
Major agricultural exporters do have a history of invoking emergency protectionist measures during severe climate shocks.
Context
The announcement allegedly surfaced just as commodity markets closed for the weekend, triggering panic-buying among European roasters.
Defense
Lean into real anxieties about frost in South America and shifting weather patterns to make sudden government intervention sound inevitable.
cards.whyItWorks: Attaches a fabricated specific (a 50% ban) to a real general trend (climate pressure on coffee). The weekend timing conveniently explains why nobody can verify it yet.

cards.headline: Major social media platforms announce a mandatory monthly subscription fee for users who wish to keep their data hidden from corporate AI training models.
clues: Precedent
Tech firms face heavy regulatory pressure over content scraping, and analysts speculate constantly about future monetisation tiers.
Context
The change was supposedly leaked via an internal memo describing a tiered model for accounts seeking full opt-out protection.
Defense
Frame it as the logical endpoint of platform economics — if they can monetise your data, they can charge you to stop.
cards.whyItWorks: Cynicism substitutes for evidence. “Of course they would” feels like confirmation. The unnamed leaked memo is unfalsifiable by design.

cards.headline: World Health Organization issues a global warning advising citizens to avoid plastic water bottles left in direct sunlight due to a newly discovered neurotoxin.
clues: Precedent
Health agencies do issue warnings about microplastics and chemical leaching under thermal stress.
Context
The alert was allegedly distributed via an emergency bulletin about bottled water left in hot vehicles.
Defense
Use terminology about polymer breakdown and chemical toxicity to suggest a suppressed safety warning finally surfacing.
cards.whyItWorks: A real forwarded-message hoax with a decade of circulation. Borrowing a genuine agency's authority for an invented finding is the most common health-misinformation pattern there is.

cards.headline: The European Union passes legislation requiring all smartphone manufacturers to include a built-in breathalyser that disables messaging apps after midnight.
clues: Precedent
The EU genuinely does pass aggressive standardised hardware mandates on manufacturers selling into the bloc, such as the USB-C charging requirement.
Context
The regulation was reportedly driven by transport safety committees seeking to curb late-night incidents.
Defense
Argue that EU regulators prioritise public safety over convenience and that hardware-level safety integration is becoming normal.
cards.whyItWorks: One true precedent (USB-C) is used to license an absurd extrapolation. Test the leap, not the premise.

cards.headline: NASA confirms a newly discovered asteroid is composed entirely of solid platinum and will pass close enough to Earth to be mined with standard commercial rockets by 2030.
clues: Precedent
Agencies have genuinely mapped near-Earth metallic asteroids valued in the trillions.
Context
The timeline was supposedly fast-tracked after a rocket startup secured a multi-billion-dollar defence subsidy.
Defense
Hype the commercial stakes and the billionaire space race; insist the interception technology already exists.
cards.whyItWorks: “Composed entirely of solid platinum” and “standard commercial rockets” are both quietly impossible, buried under a real research programme.

cards.headline: The Netherlands will convert every motorway lane to load-bearing solar panels by 2032, funding the rollout entirely from the electricity generated.
clues: Precedent
The country genuinely piloted a solar cycle path, and its infrastructure agency has a real reputation for experimental road technology.
Context
The programme was reportedly approved after a pilot stretch outperformed rooftop installations in winter output.
Defense
Emphasise the self-funding mechanism — once a road pays for itself, no politician needs to justify the budget.
cards.whyItWorks: A real, tiny pilot inflated to a national mandate. The self-funding claim removes the obvious objection before anyone raises it.

cards.headline: Airlines will begin charging passengers by combined body and baggage weight from 2027 under new international fuel-efficiency rules.
clues: Precedent
Fuel burn genuinely scales with total aircraft weight, and airlines already price checked baggage by the kilogram.
Context
The scheme was reportedly agreed at an industry association summit as part of emissions-reduction commitments.
Defense
Argue the physics is undeniable and that extending existing baggage pricing to total load is merely consistent.
cards.whyItWorks: The underlying physics is true, so the policy inherits its credibility. The invented part is that any regulator mandated it.

cards.headline: Japan becomes the first country to make a four-day working week legally mandatory for all employers, with criminal penalties for violations.
clues: Precedent
The Japanese government genuinely has published guidance encouraging shorter working weeks, and the country has real, well-documented overwork legislation.
Context
The law was reportedly accelerated by demographic pressure and a series of high-profile overwork cases.
Defense
Point to Japan's existing overtime caps as proof that this government legislates working hours aggressively.
cards.whyItWorks: Converts a real recommendation into a fabricated mandate. The distinction between “encouraged” and “required” is where most policy misinformation lives.

cards.headline: UNESCO adds internet memes to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, recognising them as a protected form of global folk expression.
clues: Precedent
The Intangible Cultural Heritage list genuinely covers oral traditions, social practices and folk expression rather than physical monuments.
Context
The listing was reportedly proposed by a bloc of member states seeking recognition for digital-native culture.
Defense
Argue memes are demonstrably folk expression transmitted culturally — a textbook fit for the category as it is actually defined.
cards.whyItWorks: The category genuinely almost fits, which is the trap. Plausible categorisation is not evidence that a nomination occurred; inscriptions come from named states, in named sessions, on the record.

cards.headline: Several countries move to impose a nightly screen curfew for under-16s after a study linked blue light to permanent retinal cell damage.
clues: Precedent
Multiple governments have genuinely legislated minimum ages and time limits for minors' social media access.
Context
The curfew was reportedly triggered by an ophthalmology study circulated ahead of peer review.
Defense
Combine real parental anxiety about screen time with clinical-sounding language about photoreceptor degradation.
cards.whyItWorks: A real legislative trend plus an invented medical justification. “Circulated ahead of peer review” is doing all the work — it explains away the absence of a citation.
